title: Knowledge Graph Construction
blurb: Tests the extraction pipeline from text to graph, why entity extraction is easier than relation extraction, rule-based brittleness, ontology validation as a precision tool, LLM extraction for sentence shapes rules miss, and how precision and recall moved stage by stage.

questions.prompt: What are the three stages of knowledge-graph construction in this chapter?
options: Tokenisation, embedding, then clustering
Crawling, indexing, then ranking
Labelling, training, then deployment
Entities, relations, then validation
questions.explanation: Each stage can fail on its own, for different reasons, which is why the chapter measures them separately.

questions.prompt: Why did the regex extract "Jane Doe previously" as a subject?
options: The ontology listed "Jane Doe previously" as a person.
The word "previously" was capitalised in the source text.
The regex couldn't tell where the name ended.
The LLM step added the extra word.
questions.explanation: The non-greedy group stopped at the first literal boundary, which came after the adverb. Pattern matching without structure fails this way.

refLinks.label: §78.2.1 Rule-Based Extraction Is Cheap, Transparent, and Brittle: All Three at Once

questions.prompt: Why was relation extraction harder than entity extraction here?
options: Entities were labelled by hand and relations weren't.
Relations need exact phrase boundaries.
The relation patterns were written in a different language.
Relations are always rarer than entities in any text.
questions.explanation: Entities scored 1.000 precision and recall. Relations scored 0.800 and 0.571 on the same corpus.

refLinks.label: §78.2.1 Rule-Based Extraction Is Cheap, Transparent, and Brittle: All Three at Once

questions.prompt: What does an ontology domain/range check do?
options: Adds facts the extractor missed
Drops triples with the wrong types
Renames entities to a standard spelling
Merges duplicate relations into one
questions.explanation: WORKED_AT must run from a PERSON to an ORG. A triple that breaks that is removed.

refLinks.label: §78.2.2 Ontology Validation Fixes Precision, Not Recall: and That Split Is the Point

questions.prompt: Why can validation raise precision but never recall?
options: Recall is fixed by the size of the gold set.
It ignores triples that pass the schema.
It can only delete, never add.
It only runs on entities, not relations.
questions.explanation: After validation, precision rose to 1.000 while recall stayed at 0.571. The correct Jane Doe fact was never produced, so nothing could keep it.

refLinks.label: §78.2.2 Ontology Validation Fixes Precision, Not Recall: and That Split Is the Point

options: Treating validation as a fix for low recall
Dropping triples with unknown entities
Checking subject and object types against the schema
Running validation after rule-based extraction
questions.explanation: Validation removes bad triples. Low recall needs a better extractor for the gap.

questions.prompt: Which sentence did the LLM step target?
options: The Jane Doe sentence with the boundary bug
A passive sentence no regex covered
A sentence with a misspelled company name
Every sentence, replacing the rule-based extractor
questions.explanation: The LLM handled a shape no pattern was written for. The Jane Doe error stayed, since nothing revisited it.

questions.prompt: What does Procedure 78.3 say about trusting LLM extractions?
options: Trust them, since a larger model makes fewer errors.
Run the same validation as for rule-based output.
Use them only when the regex finds nothing at all.
Skip validation if the JSON parses cleanly.
questions.explanation: LLM output can be malformed or hallucinated. It needs the same consistency check as any other source.

questions.prompt: When is a small, fixed ontology the right choice?
options: For open-domain text where relevant relations aren't known yet
Whenever the corpus is larger than a million documents
Whenever an LLM is used for extraction
For a domain whose types are known in advance
questions.explanation: A fixed schema enables domain/range checks. Open-domain extraction has weaker validation, since there's nothing fixed to check against.

questions.prompt: After adding the LLM's facts, 6 of 7 gold relations were found. What is recall? Give three decimal places.
Raw relation extraction predicted 5 triples, 4 of them correct. What was its precision?
questions.explanation: 4 / 5 = 0.800. The wrong one was ("Jane Doe previously", WORKED_AT, "Initech").

questions.prompt: What does the chapter's full trace (0.800/0.571, then 1.000/0.571, then 1.000/0.857) show?
options: The LLM step made precision worse.
Validation improved recall more than the LLM did.
Precision and recall move independently.
One accuracy figure would have shown the same thing.
questions.explanation: Validation fixed precision, the LLM fixed part of recall. A single number would hide which stage did what.

bookExercises.prompt: Name the three pipeline stages of knowledge graph construction from text (entity recognition, relation extraction, validation), and state which one can only remove predictions, never add them.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Entity recognition, relation extraction, validation. Validation can only remove predictions (drop triples that fail a consistency check), never add new ones.

bookExercises.prompt: State the measured entity precision/recall (1.000/1.000) and raw relation precision/recall (0.800/0.571) from the Worked Example, and explain in one sentence why the two tasks measured so differently on the same corpus.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Entities: precision 1.000, recall 1.000. Raw relations: precision 0.800, recall 0.571. The two tasks measured so differently because entity extraction only needs to recognise that a capitalised span with a known suffix is an entity, while relation extraction additionally needs to get phrase *boundaries* exactly right (subject and object spans), which is a harder, more error-prone problem, as shown by the "Jane Doe previously" boundary bug.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's validation-step result (precision 0.800→1.000, recall 0.571→0.571, unchanged), explain concretely why this specific pattern (precision improving, recall exactly flat) is the expected signature of a validation-only fix, and what a DIFFERENT pattern (e.g. both precision and recall improving) would have implied instead.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Precision improving while recall stays exactly flat is the expected signature of a validation-only fix because validation's only possible action is removing bad predictions. Removing a false positive (like the malformed "Jane Doe previously" triple) directly improves precision (fewer wrong predictions among those kept) without touching which correct facts were ever produced in the first place, which is what recall measures. A different pattern, both precision AND recall improving, would imply the intervention did something beyond filtering: either producing new correct predictions (which validation alone structurally cannot do) or correcting a previously wrong prediction into a right one, neither of which a pure consistency check can accomplish.

bookExercises.prompt: Using the Worked Example's full pipeline trace (entities 1.000/1.000; relations 0.800/0.571 → 1.000/0.571 → 1.000/0.857), explain why final recall (0.857) is still below 1.000 even after both validation and LLM extraction were applied. What specific, still-uncorrected error is responsible?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Final recall (0.857) stays below 1.000 because the earlier `("Jane Doe previously", "WORKED_AT", "Initech")` boundary error is still uncorrected. That triple was dropped by validation (fixing precision) but the correct `("Jane Doe", "WORKED_AT", "Initech")` fact was never produced by any stage of the pipeline, since neither validation nor the LLM extraction pass (which only reprocessed the ONE sentence with the missed passive-voice/implicit relation) ever revisited that specific extraction. The LLM step's improvement is scoped to the sentence it targeted; it has no mechanism to notice or fix a different, earlier mistake elsewhere in the pipeline.

bookExercises.prompt: A team reports "we validated our knowledge graph extraction and precision is now 100%, so the graph is complete and accurate." Using this chapter's Worked Example, write the two or three sentences you'd say about what that claim is missing.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: "This chapter's own pipeline trace shows precision and recall are controlled by different, independent parts of the extraction pipeline. Validation raised precision from 0.800 to 1.000 while recall stayed flat at 0.571, meaning a third of the true relationships in the corpus were still missing from the graph even after precision hit 100%. A '100% precision' claim says every kept prediction is correct, but says nothing about how many correct facts were never extracted in the first place. The graph could still be substantially incomplete even while being fully accurate on what it does contain."

bookExercises.prompt: Procedure 78.3 warns against trusting LLM output without the same validation pass applied to rule-based output. Describe a concrete way an LLM extraction could produce a plausible-looking but structurally invalid triple that Procedure 78.2's domain/range check would catch.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: An LLM could plausibly extract a relation like `("Acme Corp", "WORKED_AT", "Globex Inc")`: grammatically and semantically plausible-sounding text, but structurally invalid under the domain/range schema, since `WORKED_AT` requires a `PERSON` subject and `Acme Corp` is typed as `ORG`, not `PERSON`. Procedure 78.2's validation check would catch this by looking up `Acme Corp`'s known entity type and comparing it against `WORKED_AT`'s expected subject type (`PERSON`), rejecting the triple regardless of how confident or fluent the LLM's phrasing was, exactly the same mechanism that caught the rule-based extractor's boundary error, applied without favouritism to the extraction source.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about complex/learned embedding-based approaches to relation extraction and link prediction (e.g. Trouillon et al., "Complex Embeddings for Simple Link Prediction," referenced in this chapter's Further Reading). Explain in your own words how a learned approach might address this chapter's specific boundary-detection failure mode ("Jane Doe previously") differently than either the rule-based or LLM-prompting approaches here.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A learned embedding-based approach (e.g. representing entities and relations as vectors and scoring candidate triples by a learned compatibility function) doesn't rely on discrete text-span boundaries at all. Instead of extracting exact character spans from a sentence (where "Jane Doe previously" vs. "Jane Doe" is a hard, brittle boundary decision), it could learn to recognise "Jane Doe" as the correct entity by its similarity to other known PERSON entities in embedding space, sidestepping the specific brittle-regex-boundary failure mode entirely. This comes at the cost of needing substantial training data to learn good embeddings and losing the rule-based approach's complete auditability. A learned model's "why did it choose this boundary" is much harder to inspect directly than a regex pattern's explicit failure.
